YouTube description seed: That alarm on your ceiling has a secret. Guess what it is. #TellMeWhyyyyyy #Shorts
The central fact: Ionization smoke alarms use a tiny americium-241 source to ionize air; smoke disrupts the current and triggers the alarm.
The later surprise: The sealed source is considered safe under normal use.
The very first frame shows a white smoke alarm on a ceiling as a wisp of smoke drifts toward it. Nothing in the first second gives the answer away.
Hook test: A (statement) = "Many smoke alarms have radioactive material inside."; B (question) = "What's hiding inside your smoke alarm?".
Fact boundaries: Only ionization alarms; photoelectric ones have none. Never suggest opening an alarm; use stock footage of the inside.

facts.statement: Ionization smoke detectors contain a small americium-241 source that ionizes air in a chamber; smoke reduces the current and sets off the alarm.
The radiation dose from an ionization smoke detector in normal use is very small.

factBoundaries: Only ionization alarms; photoelectric ones have none.
Never suggest opening an alarm; use stock footage of the inside.

lockedVoiceover: Many smoke alarms have radioactive material inside.
Inside this type, there's a small metal can.
A tiny bit of americium charges the air, so a small current flows.
Smoke blocks that current, and the drop sets off the alarm.
